title: Short or long (Berakhot 34a)
hookLine: one student prays long, another short; Rabbi Eliezer says Moses did both
tomorrow: how could a sage tell his prayer for the sick got through?

lines: A BOOK OF PSALMS, AN HOUR.
cards: A hospital waiting room, early morning. One relative has a book of psalms open and plans to read for an hour. Another says one sentence, quietly, and puts her coffee down.

A third person is annoyed with both of them. So which does a scared family need, the long prayer or the short one? The Talmud has a scene with exactly this argument in it, and it refuses to pick a side.

teach.b: A student goes up to lead the prayer in front of Rabbi Eliezer, and he goes long. Really long. The other students mutter: how drawn out he is.
Rabbi Eliezer says: is he longer than Moses?
Moses lay before God forty days and forty nights, pleading for his people. Then another student leads, and he's quick.
The students mutter again: how short he is. Rabbi Eliezer says: is he shorter than Moses?
When his sister Miriam was struck ill, Moses prayed in one breath: "Heal her now, O God, I beseech Thee." Here are the two views, at their best. The long camp: some things need staying.
A people's whole future, a grief, a fear that doesn't fit in a sentence. Leaving early can be its own kind of leaving.

The short camp: when someone you love is sick in front of you, a long speech can be about you. Moses didn't make a speech for Miriam; he asked, plainly, and stopped. Rabbi Eliezer doesn't call either student wrong.
He holds up one teacher who did both, at different moments. So the question was never long or short. It's what this moment is asking for.

how: In Jewish practice, prayers for the sick range from Moses' few words for Miriam to reading many psalms together; communities also say the Mi Shebeirach, a prayer for healing, naming the sick person.

o: a prayer's length should fit what the moment is asking
long prayers count more, the way Moses prayed forty days
keep prayers brief, since God already knows what you mean

games.q: two complaints, two answers — tap the pairs.
p: shorter than Moses? heal her now

s: the Talmud teaches that a longer prayer is a holier prayer
Rabbi Eliezer defends the short one too, with Moses' one line for Miriam.
Moses' prayer for his sick sister is a single line
"Heal her now, O God, I beseech Thee."

games.q: a friend's dad is in the ER. in the group chat, one person wants to plan a long candle vigil tonight; another says just send her one line. what would Rabbi Eliezer say?
o: go long: a big vigil shows how much everyone cares.
go short: long gestures are always about the people giving them.
ask what she needs right now; Moses did both, at different moments.
games.why: Rabbi Eliezer doesn't rule for one length. he points at Moses, who prayed forty days for his people and one line for his sick sister.

practice: Bring one person to mind who needs something right now. Ask what this moment needs: one plain sentence for them, said out loud and left alone, or the whole sit spent holding them in mind.
Do whichever it is, and don't apologize for the length.

wordCard.voice: Short or long. Rabbi Eliezer's answer to both complaints: Moses prayed forty days, and Moses prayed one line.

orig.note: Hebrew: Numbers 12:13, Moses' prayer for Miriam: heal her now, O God, I beseech Thee.

carryVoice: For the pocket: short or long, as needed, the way Moses had both in him. More tomorrow.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 34a (a student prays long and another short before Rabbi Eliezer; Moses' forty days and his prayer for Miriam)

sources.q: Heal her now, O God, I beseech Thee.
